mainTopic: The size and awareness requirements of עירובי תבשילין, and making other עירובין on a יום טוב that falls on ערב שבת
overview: This amud opens with the last line of an earlier discussion about בישולי עכו"ם: in a fish-and-flour dish, the flour is the main ingredient. Then רבי אבא rules that an עירובי תבשילין needs a כזית of food. One כזית covers any number of people. Two challenges, from the משנה and from a ברייתא, are answered: there is no maximum size, but there is a minimum of a כזית. Next, רב rules that an עירובי תבשילין needs דעת, and the גמרא asks whether the people it is made for must also know about it. It brings rabbis who made one עירוב for a whole city, and the story of שמואל, who would not let a habitually negligent student rely on his עירוב. A ברייתא then discusses making עירובי תחומין and עירובי חצרות on a יום טוב that falls on ערב שבת. רבי allows עירובי חצרות, and רב and שמואל disagree whose view is the הלכה. Because of רבי אלעזר's report that the opinions are reversed, the גמרא asks whether ruling like רבי is lenient or strict. It tries to prove the answer from רב's complaint of 'ruin', and begins to push back on that proof, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Flour is the main ingredient of the fish-and-flour dish
steps.stepSummary: The tail end of the previous discussion. You might have thought the fish fat (הרסנא) is the main part of the dish, so the ruling teaches that the flour is the main part.
steps.simpleTranslation: [You might have thought that] the fish fat is the main ingredient. So it teaches us that the flour is the main ingredient.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an earlier discussion about a dish of small fish fried with flour by a non-Jew. It explains that the ruling was needed to teach that the flour, not the fish, is the main ingredient.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier ruling forbade this dish because of בישולי עכו"ם. Someone could have asked why the ruling was even necessary. The answer: we might have thought the fish fat sets the status of the dish, and fish fat cooked by a non-Jew is permitted. The ruling teaches that the flour is what counts, so the dish is a new, significant food and is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: Small fish fried in their fat, often mixed with flour
'It teaches us' — introduces the new point a ruling is coming to make

steps.confusionAlert: This line belongs to the previous topic (בישולי עכו"ם). It has nothing to do with עירובי תבשילין, which starts in the next line.

phrases.english: the fish fat is the main ingredient,
phrases.notes: End of the 'you might have thought' line (מהו דתימא), which began earlier

phrases.english: it teaches us that the flour is the main ingredient.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes a discussion earlier
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explaining what new point the ruling makes
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The fish fat is the main ingredient, so the dish would be permitted
steps.terutzMaskana: The flour is the main ingredient, so the dish is forbidden

steps.title: An עירובי תבשילין needs a כזית
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא rules that an עירובי תבשילין must contain at least a כזית of food.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא said: An עירובי תבשילין requires an olive-bulk of food.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. רבי אבא gives a size requirement for the cooked food used in an עירובי תבשילין: it must be at least a כזית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An עירובי תבשילין lets a person cook on יום טוב for שבת that comes right after it. רבי אבא adds a minimum size: a tiny crumb of food does not work. The rest of this passage tests and clarifies this rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Cooked food set aside before יום טוב that allows cooking on יום טוב for שבת
An olive-bulk, a basic halachic minimum size

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the base rule for the whole passage. Every question and challenge that follows is about this כזית requirement.

phrases.english: Rabbi Abba said:
An eiruv of cooked foods requires an olive-bulk.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic, unrelated to the previous line
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An עירובי תבשילין must have at least a כזית of food

steps.title: One olive-bulk for everyone, or one for each person?
steps.stepSummary: The scholars ask whether a single כזית covers everyone relying on the עירוב, or whether each person needs their own כזית.
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked: Is one olive-bulk enough for all of them, or perhaps there must be an olive-bulk for each and every person?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts רבי אבא's כזית rule and asks a follow-up question about how it applies when many people rely on one עירוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If many people are relying on one person's עירוב, it is not clear whether the כזית is a single requirement for the whole עירוב. The alternative is that each person counts separately, so ten people would need ten כזיתים. This is a genuine question, not an attack.

keyTerms.meaning: 'A question was asked before them' — introduces a genuine halachic question

phrases.english: A question was raised before them:
one olive-bulk for all of them,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא כְּזַיִת לְכׇל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד?
phrases.english: or perhaps an olive-bulk for each and every one?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how far רבי אבא's כזית rule reaches
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the כזית requirement apply once per עירוב, or once per person relying on it?

steps.title: One olive-bulk works for one person or a hundred
steps.stepSummary: The answer comes from רבי אבא quoting רב: one כזית is enough whether the עירוב is for one person or for a hundred.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: רבי אבא said in the name of רב: An עירובי תבשילין requires an olive-bulk, whether for one person or for one hundred.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by quoting a fuller version of the rule, in רב's name. One כזית is enough no matter how many people rely on it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'whether for one, whether for a hundred' settle the question directly. The כזית is a requirement on the עירוב itself, not on each person. So a single כזית covers everyone.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Come and hear' — introduces a source that answers or proves something

steps.whatToRemember: An עירובי תבשילין needs one כזית total, and that single כזית covers any number of people.

phrases.english: Come and hear,
for Rabbi Abba said that Rav said:
An eiruv of cooked foods requires an olive-bulk
whether for one, whether for a hundred.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע, דְּאָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from Step 3
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A single כזית is enough for any number of people

steps.title: Challenge from the משנה: 'any amount' left over is enough
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the כזית rule from the משנה, which says that if any amount (כל שהוא) of the עירוב is left, one may still rely on it. That seems to show that even less than a כזית works.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in the משנה: If he ate it or it was lost, he may not begin cooking based on it. If he left any amount of it, he may rely on it for שבת. What does 'any amount' mean? Doesn't it mean even if there is not an olive-bulk?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a משנה that seems to contradict רבי אבא. The משנה says that a leftover of 'any amount' is still valid, which suggests that no כזית is needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה separates two cases. If the עירוב was entirely eaten or lost, one cannot rely on it. If some of it remains, even 'כל שהוא', one can. The phrase 'כל שהוא' usually means even a tiny amount, which would clash with the requirement of a כזית.

keyTerms.meaning: 'We learned' in a משנה — introduces a quote from the משנה
He ate it or it was lost
Any amount at all, even something tiny
'Is it not?' — opens a suggested reading that creates a difficulty

phrases.english: We learned in the Mishnah:
If he ate it or it was lost —
he may not begin cooking based on it,
if he left any amount of it —
he may rely on it for Shabbat.
What does 'any amount' mean?

phrases.aramaic: לָאו אַף עַל גַּב דְּלֵיכָּא כְּזַיִת?
phrases.english: Doesn't it mean even though there is not an olive-bulk?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to challenge the basic כזית rule itself
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אבא's rule that the עירוב needs a כזית
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה's words 'כל שהוא' seem to allow a leftover smaller than a כזית

steps.title: 'Any amount' still means at least an olive-bulk
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that 'כל שהוא' in the משנה refers to a leftover that still contains a כזית.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it means that there is still an olive-bulk in it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the reading that challenged רבי אבא. The משנה's 'any amount' still assumes a כזית remains.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's point is that even a small remnant of the original עירוב is enough, as long as it is still a כזית. 'כל שהוא' describes how little is left compared to the original, not a size below the halachic minimum. So the כזית rule stands.
steps.confusionAlert: Here 'כל שהוא' does not mean a tiny crumb. It means 'only a little is left', while still being at least a כזית.

phrases.english: No, it means there is an olive-bulk in it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 5
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting a word in the source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'כל שהוא' means even less than a כזית
steps.terutzMaskana: 'כל שהוא' means a small leftover that is still a כזית

steps.title: Challenge from a ברייתא: the עירוב has 'no measure'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא listing which cooked foods qualify. It says the עירוב has no שיעור at the beginning or the end, which seems to mean no minimum size at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: A cooked dish can be roasted, or even pickled, well-boiled, or regularly cooked, or even Spanish soft fish that had hot water poured on it before יום טוב. At its beginning and at its end it has no set measure. Doesn't that mean it has no measure at all?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי אבא again, this time from a ברייתא. The ברייתא says the עירוב 'has no measure', which sounds like no כזית is needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא first lists the kinds of cooking that qualify: roasting, pickling, heavy boiling, normal cooking, and even a fish that was only scalded with hot water. Then it says that neither at the start nor after part was eaten or lost does the עירוב have a שיעור. Read simply, this rules out any size requirement and contradicts the כזית rule.

keyTerms.meaning: A soft Spanish fish, made edible by pouring hot water over it
Its beginning and its end (its size at the start, and after part is used up)

phrases.english: Come and hear:
A cooked dish — this includes roasted,
and even pickled, well-boiled, and regularly cooked,
and Spanish soft fish

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁנָּתַן עָלָיו חַמִּין מֵעֶרֶב יוֹם טוֹב —
phrases.english: on which he poured hot water on the eve of Yom Tov —
at its beginning and its end it has no measure.

phrases.aramaic: מַאי לָאו, אֵין לוֹ שִׁיעוּר כְּלָל?
phrases.english: What, is it not that it has no measure at all?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second challenge to the כזית rule, from a different source
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אבא's rule that the עירוב needs a כזית
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'אין לו שיעור' seems to deny any minimum size

steps.title: No maximum, but there is a minimum
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that 'no measure' means no upper limit. There is still a lower limit, the כזית.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it has no upper measure, but it does have a lower measure.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the challenge. The ברייתא's 'no measure' only means there is no maximum size, while a minimum of a כזית still applies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'אין לו שיעור' is limited to one direction. You never need more than a certain amount, even for many people, which fits רב's 'whether for one, whether for a hundred'. But you can never go below a כזית, so רבי אבא's rule survives both challenges.
steps.whatToRemember: Final picture: an עירובי תבשילין needs at least a כזית, both at the start and in whatever is left over. There is no maximum, and one כזית covers any number of people.

phrases.english: No, it has no upper measure,
but it does have a lower measure.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 7
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the phrase to one direction (maximum only)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'אין לו שיעור' means no size requirement at all
steps.terutzMaskana: There is no maximum size, but a minimum of a כזית applies

steps.title: עירובי תבשילין Require Awareness
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא quotes רב: עירובי תבשילין need דעת.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said in the name of רב: An עירוב of cooked foods needs awareness.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a ruling from רב. An עירובי תבשילין only works if there is awareness (דעת) behind it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the discussion was about the size of the עירוב (the כזית). Now the focus moves to the people involved. The ruling says the עירוב is not just an object sitting there. It needs a person's intention and awareness to work.

keyTerms.meaning: the 'joining of cooked foods' made before יום טוב so that one may cook on יום טוב for שבת

phrases.english: Rav Huna said that Rav said:
A joining of cooked foods requires awareness.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the size of the עירוב (steps 2-8) to a new requirement: awareness.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: עירובי תבשילין require דעת in order to work.

steps.title: Whose Awareness Is Needed?
steps.stepSummary: The awareness of the one who sets it up is obvious. Is the awareness of the people it is made for also needed?
steps.simpleTranslation: It is obvious that we need the awareness of the one who sets it down. Do we also need the awareness of the one it was set down for, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא clarifies רב's ruling by asking a precise question. Everyone agrees the person who prepares the עירוב must know what he is doing. The question is whether the people he is making it for must also know.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word פשיטא removes the easy case: the מניח (the one who prepares it) obviously needs awareness. The real question is about the beneficiaries. Must they know about it, or can someone make an עירוב for them without their knowledge?

keyTerms.meaning: the one who sets down (prepares) the עירוב
the one for whom it was set down (the beneficiary)

phrases.english: It is obvious that we require the awareness of the one who sets it down;
phrases.notes: This part is taken as obvious and not in question.

phrases.english: do we require the awareness of the one for whom it was set down,
or do we not require it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks exactly which awareness רב's ruling refers to.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Must the beneficiaries of an עירובי תבשילין know about it, or is only the preparer's awareness needed?
steps.confusionAlert: The question is not whether the preparer needs awareness. That is obvious. The question is only about the people the עירוב is made for.

steps.title: Rabbis Who Made an עירוב for Whole Cities
steps.stepSummary: Reports that שמואל's father, רבי אמי and רבי אסי made עירובין for entire cities, and that רבי יעקב בר אידי publicly announced that people could rely on his.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: שמואל's father would make an עירוב for all of נהרדעא. רבי אמי and רבי אסי would make an עירוב for all of טבריה. רבי יעקב בר אידי would announce: Whoever did not set down an עירובי תבשילין should come and rely on mine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings real-life practice as evidence for the question. Great rabbis made one עירוב that covered a whole city, and one rabbi publicly announced it so people would know they could rely on it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Making an עירוב for a whole city shows that one person can make it for others. The public announcement is the key detail for our question, because it suggests the beneficiaries were meant to know about it. The commentators discuss exactly what this evidence proves, since the גמרא does not state a conclusion in words here.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
Shmuel's father would make an eiruv for all of Neharde'a,

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי אַמֵּי וְרַבִּי אַסִּי מְעָרְבִי אַכּוּלַּהּ טְבֶרְיָא.
phrases.english: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi would make an eiruv for all of Tiberias.
Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi would announce:
Whoever did not set down a joining of cooked foods
should come and rely on mine.
phrases.notes: The public announcement suggests the beneficiaries were meant to know.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: דַּאֲבוּהּ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל מְעָרֵב אַכּוּלַּהּ נְהַרְדְּעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings evidence from practice to answer the question of step 10.
steps.raayaObject: Whether the beneficiaries' awareness is needed for an עירובי תבשילין made on their behalf.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The practice of שמואל's father, רבי אמי and רבי אסי, and the public announcement of רבי יעקב בר אידי.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the basis for the practice that a town rabbi makes one עירובי תבשילין for the whole community.

steps.title: How Far Does a Shared עירוב Reach?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how far away a person can be and still rely on someone else's עירוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: And up to how far?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a follow-up question about the rabbis' city-wide עירוב. How far away from it can someone live and still be covered?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once we know one person's עירוב can cover others, we need a limit. Otherwise it could seem to cover people anywhere in the world. The גמרא asks for that distance.

keyTerms.meaning: and up to how much / how far?

phrases.english: And up to how far?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the range of the shared עירוב described in step 11.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The maximum distance at which one may rely on another person's עירובי תבשילין.

steps.title: Up to the תחום שבת
steps.stepSummary: רב נחומי בר זכריה quotes אביי: a person may rely on it up to the distance of the תחום שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחומי בר זכריה said in the name of אביי: Up to the תחום שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the answer. People living within the תחום שבת of the עירוב may rely on it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The limit is taken from a familiar measure, the תחום שבת (2,000 אמות). Someone living farther away than that is not covered by this person's עירוב.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב נְחוּמִי בַּר זְכַרְיָה מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּאַבָּיֵי:
phrases.english: Rav Nechumi bar Zecharya said in the name of Abaye:
Up to the Shabbat boundary.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נְחוּמִי בַּר זְכַרְיָה מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּאַבָּיֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: One may rely on another's עירובי תבשילין if one is within the תחום שבת.

steps.title: שמואל Lets a Sad Student Rely on His עירוב
steps.stepSummary: A blind student of שמואל was sad because he had not made an עירובי תבשילין. שמואל told him to rely on his.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a blind man who used to recite משניות before מר שמואל. שמואל saw that he was sad and asked him: Why are you sad? He answered: Because I did not set down an עירובי תבשילין. שמואל said to him: Rely on mine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that shows the idea of relying on someone else's עירוב in action. שמואל kindly includes his forgetful student in his own עירוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story confirms in practice that a great rabbi's עירוב can cover others who forgot. Here the student learns about it from שמואל directly, so he knows he is relying on it.

phrases.english: There was a certain blind man

phrases.aramaic: דַּהֲוָה מְסַדַּר מַתְנְיָתָא קַמֵּיהּ דְּמָר שְׁמוּאֵל,
phrases.english: who would recite mishnayot before Mar Shmuel.
Shmuel saw that he was sad.
He said to him: Why are you sad?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: דְּלָא אוֹתִיבִי עֵרוּבֵי תַבְשִׁילִין.
phrases.english: He said to him: Because I did not set down a joining of cooked foods.
He said to him: Rely on mine.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא סַמְיָא דַּהֲוָה מְסַדַּר מַתְנְיָתָא קַמֵּיהּ דְּמָר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates in a story the practice of relying on another's עירוב described in step 11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone who forgot to make an עירובי תבשילין may rely on a rabbi's עירוב made for others.

steps.title: The Negligent Student Is Excluded
steps.stepSummary: The next year the student forgot again. שמואל called him negligent: everyone else may rely on his עירוב, but not him.
steps.simpleTranslation: The next year שמואל saw that he was sad again and asked him: Why are you sad? He answered: Because I did not set down an עירובי תבשילין. שמואל said to him: You are negligent. For everyone else it is permitted, but for you it is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues and reaches its point. A communal עירוב is meant for people who forgot by accident, not for people who keep neglecting the מצוה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since an עירוב depends on the intention (דעת) of the one who makes it, שמואל can decide whom it covers. He intended it for ordinary people who forgot, not for someone who keeps relying on it on purpose. This ties the story back to רב's rule in step 9 that עירובי תבשילין need awareness.

phrases.english: The next year he saw that he was sad.
He said to him: Why are you sad?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: דְּלָא אוֹתִיבִי עֵרוּבֵי תַּבְשִׁילִין.
phrases.english: He said to him: Because I did not set down a joining of cooked foods.
He said to him: You are negligent.
For everyone else it is permitted,
but for you it is forbidden.
phrases.notes: שמואל did not intend his עירוב to include someone who keeps neglecting the מצוה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story with an exception: a repeatedly negligent person is not included.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A communal עירובי תבשילין covers those who forgot, but not someone who is habitually negligent.
steps.whatToRemember: One person can make an עירובי תבשילין for others within the תחום שבת. It works through his intention, so it covers people who forgot by accident, not someone who keeps neglecting it on purpose.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the idea that one should not knowingly rely on the rabbi's communal עירוב instead of making one's own.

steps.title: No Other עירובין on a יום טוב Before שבת
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: when יום טוב falls on ערב שבת, one may not make עירובי תחומין or עירובי חצרות on that day.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: When יום טוב falls on ערב שבת, one may not make either an עירובי תחומין or an עירובי חצרות.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new ברייתא about other kinds of עירוב. This opens a new discussion that the גמרא will continue to examine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These two עירובין are for שבת: one is about walking distance and one is about carrying. The ברייתא rules that they cannot be set up on the יום טוב itself, even though שבת starts right after it. If one did not make them before יום טוב, it is too late.

keyTerms.meaning: an עירוב that extends one's walking boundary on שבת
an עירוב that joins courtyards so carrying is allowed on שבת

phrases.english: The Sages taught:

phrases.aramaic: יוֹם טוֹב שֶׁחָל לִהְיוֹת בְּעֶרֶב שַׁבָּת —
phrases.english: A Festival that falls on Shabbat eve —
one may not prepare an eiruv,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא עֵרוּבֵי תְחוּמִין וְלֹא עֵרוּבֵי חֲצֵרוֹת.
phrases.english: neither a joining of boundaries nor a joining of courtyards.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: יוֹם טוֹב שֶׁחָל לִהְיוֹת בְּעֶרֶב שַׁבָּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from עירובי תבשילין to other types of עירוב in the same calendar situation.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: On a יום טוב that falls on ערב שבת, one may not make עירובי תחומין or עירובי חצרות for שבת.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the three kinds of עירוב. עירובי תבשילין allows cooking for שבת on יום טוב. עירובי תחומין is about how far one may walk. עירובי חצרות is about carrying between courtyards.

steps.title: רבי allows a courtyard עירוב but not a boundary עירוב
steps.stepSummary: רבי disagrees with the תנא קמא. On a יום טוב that falls on ערב שבת, one may make עירובי חצרות but not עירובי תחומין. His reason: you may restrict someone in something already forbidden to him, but not in something permitted to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי says: On that יום טוב you may make an עירוב for courtyards, but not an עירוב for שבת boundaries. This is because you may restrict him in a matter that is already forbidden to him, but you may not restrict him in a matter that is permitted to him.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the second opinion in the same ברייתא from Step 16. רבי partly disagrees with the תנא קמא and gives a reason for treating the two kinds of עירוב differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Going past the תחום is forbidden on יום טוב just as on שבת, so making an עירובי תחומין on יום טוב would create a brand-new permission on a day when that act is forbidden. Carrying between domains is already permitted on יום טוב. So an עירובי חצרות made on יום טוב does not create a new permission for something forbidden today, and רבי allows it.

keyTerms.meaning: A joining of courtyards, which permits carrying between private domains on שבת
A joining of boundaries, which lets a person walk past the normal 2,000-אמה limit on שבת

steps.confusionAlert: The two kinds of עירוב are not the same thing. עירובי חצרות is about carrying. עירובי תחומין is about walking distance. רבי's whole distinction depends on the fact that carrying is allowed on יום טוב, while walking past the תחום is not.

phrases.english: Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) says:
one may make a joining of courtyards,
but not a joining of boundaries.

phrases.aramaic: מִפְּנֵי שֶׁאַתָּה אוֹסְרוֹ בְּדָבָר הָאָסוּר לוֹ,
phrases.english: because you may restrict him in a matter that is forbidden to him,
phrases.notes: Walking past the תחום, which is forbidden on יום טוב too

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי אַתָּה אוֹסְרוֹ בְּדָבָר הַמּוּתָּר לוֹ.
phrases.english: but you may not restrict him in a matter that is permitted to him.
phrases.notes: Carrying, which is permitted on יום טוב

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ברייתא of Step 16 by adding רבי's dissenting view.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: On a יום טוב that falls on ערב שבת, עירובי חצרות is allowed but עירובי תחומין is not.

steps.title: רב and שמואל disagree on whose view is the הלכה
steps.stepSummary: רב rules like the תנא קמא, so neither עירוב may be made. שמואל rules like רבי, so עירובי חצרות may be made.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: רב said the הלכה follows the תנא קמא. שמואל said the הלכה follows רבי.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים disagree about how to rule in practice on the ברייתא's dispute.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב follows the stricter view, which forbids both kinds of עירוב. שמואל follows רבי, which, as the ברייתא currently reads, allows עירובי חצרות. This disagreement sets up the next question.

keyTerms.meaning: It was stated, introducing a dispute between אמוראים
The first, unnamed opinion in a ברייתא or משנה
The halacha follows the view of...

phrases.english: It was stated:
Rav said: the halacha follows the first Tanna.
And Shmuel said: the halacha follows Rabbi.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִתְּמַר, רַב אָמַר: הֲלָכָה כְּתַנָּא קַמָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the practical ruling on the dispute in Steps 16–17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב: the halacha follows the תנא קמא. שמואל: the halacha follows רבי.

steps.title: Is ruling like רבי lenient or strict?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether שמואל's 'the halacha follows רבי' means a lenient ruling or a strict one.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: when שמואל says the halacha follows רבי, is that a leniency or a stringency?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a question about what שמואל's ruling actually means. The next steps will explain why this is even a question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally רבי is the lenient one here. Asking 'lenient or strict?' hints that there is doubt about what רבי actually said.

keyTerms.meaning: It was asked of them; a question the scholars raised

phrases.english: It was asked of them:
Is 'the halacha follows Rabbi' a leniency or a stringency?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the meaning of שמואל's ruling from Step 18.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does שמואל's ruling like רבי lead to a lenient result or a strict one?

steps.title: Isn't it obvious that it is lenient?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects to its own question: רבי is clearly the lenient one, so of course ruling like him is a leniency.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is obvious that he meant it as a leniency!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the question it just asked, saying the answer seems obvious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: As we just read the ברייתא, רבי allows עירובי חצרות and the תנא קמא forbids it. So following רבי must be lenient, and the question seems unnecessary.

phrases.english: It is obvious that he said it as a leniency!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether the question in Step 19 is needed at all.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא shows רבי as the lenient one, so there seems to be nothing to ask.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר's report that the opinions are reversed
steps.stepSummary: The question is real because רבי אלעזר sent word from ארץ ישראל that the ברייתא should read the other way: רבי forbids and the חכמים permit.
steps.simpleTranslation: The question arises because רבי אלעזר sent to the Diaspora: It is not as you teach in בבל, that רבי permits and the חכמים forbid. Rather, רבי forbids and the חכמים permit. So what is the ruling?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why its question is not obvious. There are two versions of the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the version reported by רבי אלעזר, רבי is the strict one. Then 'the halacha follows רבי' would be a stringency. So we need to know which version שמואל was relying on.

keyTerms.meaning: You teach or recite (the text of a ברייתא)
What? (meaning: so what is the ruling?)

steps.confusionAlert: Nothing about the law itself changed. Only who said what got swapped. The opinions stay the same; the names attached to them are reversed.

phrases.english: Because Rabbi Elazar sent to the Diaspora:
Not as you teach in Babylonia,
that Rabbi permits and the Sages forbid,
rather, Rabbi forbids and the Sages permit.
So what is the ruling?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection of Step 20 and brings back the question of Step 19.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Textual variant: a different version of the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי is clearly the lenient one, so the question is pointless.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because there is another version where רבי is strict, the question is real.

steps.title: The story of רב תחליפא בר אבדימי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries to prove the answer. רב תחליפא בר אבדימי ruled in practice like שמואל, and רב said this young scholar's first ruling was a 'ruin.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: רב תחליפא בר אבדימי acted in practice like שמואל. רב said: The first ruling of this young scholar is a ruin.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a story to answer the question. Here it only sets up the facts; the next step draws the conclusion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב held like the תנא קמא, so he disapproved of a ruling like שמואל. The key clue is his word 'ruin,' which the next step will analyze.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear; introduces a proof
He acted in practice, giving a real ruling

phrases.english: Come and hear:
that Rav Tachlifa bar Avdimi
acted in practice in accordance with Shmuel,
and Rav said:
the first ruling of this young scholar
is for ruin.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע, דְּרַב תַּחְלִיפָא בַּר אַבְדִּימִי עֲבַד עוֹבָדָא כְּוָתֵיהּ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a proof to answer the question raised in Steps 19 and 21.
steps.raayaObject: Whether ruling like שמואל and רבי is lenient
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of רב תחליפא בר אבדימי and רב's reaction to it

steps.title: 'Ruin' only fits a lenient ruling
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא analyzes רב's word. If שמואל's ruling was lenient, calling it a 'ruin' makes sense. If it was strict, what ruin could there be?
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say שמואל meant it as a leniency, that is the 'ruin.' But if you say he meant it as a stringency, what ruin is there?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws the conclusion from the story. רב's complaint shows that the ruling like שמואל was lenient.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A strict ruling can't cause anyone to sin, so it is not called 'ruin.' Only a lenient ruling that permits something forbidden, in רב's view, can be a ruin. So the proof points to 'lenient,' which matches our version of the ברייתא, where רבי permits.

keyTerms.meaning: It works well if you say...

steps.whatToRemember: This is only an attempted proof: if 'ruin' can describe only a lenient ruling, then ruling like רבי must be lenient. The next step pushes back, showing that a strict ruling can also be called a 'ruin'.

phrases.english: Granted, if you say he said it as a leniency,
that is the ruin.
But if you say it was a stringency,
what ruin is there?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the story in Step 22 proves the answer.
steps.raayaObject: Ruling like רבי, as שמואל did, is a leniency
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב calling the ruling a 'ruin,' which only fits a lenient ruling

steps.title: A strict ruling can also cause a ruin, because the public will stumble
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back on the proof from step 23. A strict ruling could also be called a 'ruin,' because it causes many people to go wrong.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since the public will be led into wrongdoing by it,
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is answering the proof from step 23. It shows that 'ruin' can describe a strict ruling too, because a strict ruling here would make the public stumble. The sentence continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 23 said: 'ruin' only makes sense if שמואל's ruling was lenient. The גמרא now says that is not necessarily true. If people are told they may not make an עירוב חצירות on יום טוב, many will skip it, and then on שבת they may carry between courtyards without an עירוב, which is a real איסור. So 'ruin' fits a strict ruling just as well, and the proof falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: They are damaged / led into wrongdoing (from the root קלקל, 'to spoil' or 'ruin')
The joining of courtyards that lets people carry between shared courtyards on שבת

steps.confusionAlert: Do not assume that 'strict' always means 'safe.' Here a strict ruling can lead people into a worse איסור. If they refrain from making the עירוב, they may come to carry on שבת without one.
steps.whyThisMatters: This teaches an important idea: a חומרא that confuses the public can lead to real sin, so it can be called a 'ruin' just like a wrong leniency.

phrases.english: Since they are led into wrongdoing
phrases.notes: The verb comes from קלקל, which echoes the word 'ruin' (קלקולא) in רב's comment.

phrases.english: by it, the many (the public),
phrases.notes: 'By it' means by the strict ruling. The comma shows that the explanation continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference in step 23 that 'ruin' can only describe a lenient ruling.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof from רב's word 'ruin' as evidence that שמואל's ruling was lenient.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed only a leniency can be a 'ruin.' But a strict ruling also causes ruin, because the public, avoiding the עירוב on יום טוב, may carry on שבת without one.
